name: Oghuz Yabgu State
summary: A state of the Oghuz Turks on the steppes north of the Aral Sea; Oghuz groups later became the Seljuks and the ancestors of the Turkmen, Turks of Turkey and Azerbaijanis.

knownFor.label: Seljuk origins
knownFor.note: The Seljuks came from the Oghuz.

location.value: Between the Caspian and Aral Seas: the lower Syr Darya and the western Kazakh steppes; the capital was Yangikent (“New City”).

terrain.value: Open grassland steppe with river valleys.

climate.value: Continental: hot summers and very cold winters.

resources.value: Pasture for horses, sheep and cattle.

disasters.value: Harsh winters (dzud) that killed herds; droughts.

population.value: Uncertain, but the Oghuz had many tribes.

urbanisation.value: Mostly nomadic camps; a few trading towns.

disease.value: Plague and epidemics carried along trade routes.

migration.value: Oghuz groups moved into Iran and Anatolia (1000s).

economicBase.value: Herding horses, sheep and cattle; tribute and raiding.

tradeRoutes.value: Trade with Khwarazm and the Samanids.

wealth.value: Wealth in herds, tribute and plunder.

moneyAndTax.value: Tribute from settled neighbours; little coinage of their own.

inequality.value: Ruling clans above commoner herders and slaves.

governmentType.value: A state ruled by a yabgu, a title below khagan; the army was led by the subaşı.

keyRulers.value: Ali Yabgu; Shahmalik, the last yabgu, who took Khwarazm (1041) and was executed by the Seljuks two years later.

succession.value: The yabgu came from a ruling clan.

institutions.value: Clan assemblies and the khan’s household.

stability.value: Popular revolts against heavy taxes around 1000; the conflict with the Seljuk branch weakened the state.

eliteConflict.value: A split with the Seljuk branch of the Oghuz, who rebelled and briefly took Jend.

majorWars.value: Allied with Kievan Rus’ against the Khazars (965) and against Volga Bulgaria (985).

alliancesRivals.value: Allied with the Karluks and Kimeks against the Kangars and Pechenegs (early 800s) and with Kievan Rus’ (965, 985); rivals of the Seljuks.

inventions.value: No major inventions are recorded; skilled horsemanship and metalwork.

scienceEducation.value: Oral learning and epic tradition (such as the later Book of Dede Korkut).

openness.value: Open to trade and alliances with settled empires.

religion.value: Steppe religion at first; by the 900s Muslim writers called the Muslim Oghuz “Turkmens”, and by the 1100s most Oghuz were Muslim.

languageWriting.value: Oghuz Turkic, ancestor of Turkish, Azerbaijani and Turkmen.

artsArchitecture.value: Little survives, apart from graves and stone figures.

dailyLife.value: Felt tents; meat, milk and fermented mare’s milk.

neighbours.value: The Karluks, Kimeks, Khazars, Pechenegs, Khwarazm and the Samanids.

ideasReligions.value: Many Oghuz converted to Islam in the 900s.

riseSignals.value: Founded by Oghuz Turks around 750; in the early 800s they took the lower Syr Darya from the Kangars and Pechenegs.

peakPeriod.value: The 900s, when the Oghuz were a major power on the steppe.

declineSignals.value: Internal turmoil, conflict with the Seljuks and the execution of the last yabgu (1043).

outcome.value: The weakened state fell to Kipchak attacks; the Seljuk branch of the Oghuz went on to found an empire.

overallCertainty.value: Known mostly from Byzantine, Chinese, Arab and Persian writers and from archaeology; numbers are estimates.
